record_type_quote: In this article, we replicate the Great Equalizer study using better test scores in both the original data and a newer cohort of children.

targets.authors: Downey, Douglas B., Paul T. von Hippel, and Beckett A. Broh.
targets.title: Are Schools the Great Equalizer? Cognitive Inequality during the Summer Months and the School Year.
targets.evidence_quote: In this article, we replicate a well-known study of growth in cognitive inequality: the article “Are Schools the Great Equalizer?” which has been cited nearly 800 times since it was published in 2004 by the American Sociological Review (Downey et al. 2004). We carry out the same analyses as in the original study, but we use betterscaled test scores that can more plausibly compare inequality at different ages. In addition, we update the Great Equalizer study with evidence from a younger cohort of children who started kindergarten 13 years after the original participants.
targets.outcome_quote: It scored reading and math with a non-interval scale, which made it appear that score gaps grew dramatically from kindergarten through first grade. This replication shows that the apparent gap growth in the Great Equalizer study was an artifact of scaling. When we measure reading and math ability with something closer to a vertical interval scale, gaps grow very little. While the contrast between school and summer still suggests that schools do something to equalize children, the amount of equalization now seems rather small compared to the inequality that exists at the start of kindergarten.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The article explicitly overturns substantial inequality growth while retaining the seasonal equalization finding, with additional seasonal patterns inconsistent across cohorts. This is partial support and partial correction. It includes reanalysis of the original cohort and a newer independent cohort; classification follows the new-sample component.
